title: Getting Better at Tough Conversations
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article reframes tough conversations as collaborative problem-solving rather than confrontation, arguing that the dread leaders feel comes from anticipating the other person's negative reaction. The author's core technique is a language shift: replacing accusatory you statements with we and I framing that signals partnership and support. Several before-and-after examples illustrate how the same difficult message lands very differently depending on whether it's framed as judgment or as a shared problem to solve. The piece concludes that leaders can't eliminate the discomfort of hard news, but they can change how it's received by changing the frame.
points: Leaders dread tough conversations mainly because they anticipate the other person's negative reaction
Reframing the conversation as a shared problem to solve, using we and I instead of you, changes how it lands
Several before-and-after phrasing examples show how the same message can feel judgmental or supportive
The negative content of a tough message can't change, but the collaborative frame reduces the sting
quotes: Holding people accountable, delivering news of unwanted change, and sharing decisions that disappoint are some of the many topics considered “tough” for leaders to navigate.

The best leaders reframe the entire conversation to change this script. Instead of viewing the conversation as confronting a difficult topic or issue, they think of it as a collaborative problem-solving exchange.
They place themselves inside the problem, issue, or news by using the pronouns “We” and “I” instead of “You.
Viewing a tough conversation as a problem to be collaboratively resolved together is automatically less judgmental and critical
Good leaders solve a problem together with the other party when they deliver a tough message.
